@martincostello
Not directly related, but when writing the extension I realised that I couldn't use the `Pool` that the pipeline was configured with as it is not a public property.

For all our current use cases we are not setting a custom context, so it is a not an immediate issue.

Should it be made public though so that extension methods, or even the standard pattern when customizing more fully using the `try..finally` pattern would allow the caller to always request from the Pool associated with the pipeline so that the decision making on the context factory to use is always made by the pipeline declaration and not per call site?

Which pool do you mean specifically? The first one that comes to mind is this one, which is public:

https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/954ad8d32a60632e1d739cedb13925013fdebded/src/Polly.Core/ResilienceContextPool.cs#L14

@martincostello - It is the internal `Pool` property on the `ResiliencePipeline` itself.
I did not trace code for where it is set, but I assume it is mapped during build when a custom `ResilienceContextPool` is set using the `ResiliencePipelineBuilderBase.ContextPool` property.

https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/blob/40b5bb62e58dca97e3e7461bcb817f4debb00c74/src/Polly.Core/ResiliencePipeline.cs#L26

I'm on the fence whether we _should_ expose it, but I can see that it would be useful in the scenario that:

1. You want to use a custom `ResilienceContextPool` implementation, and:
2. You have a custom extension method for `ResiliencePipeline` _and_ wish to access that specific custom pool in that method.

Just did a quick spike of hacking around at this locally and found the following:

- Polly v7 has a sync and an async cache, which are the consumer is expected to implement themselves as-appropriate using the provided interface. There's also some basic wrapping to handle serializing the value before caching.
- Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Abstractions provides the sync `IMemoryCache` and the async `IDistributedCache` - this is effectively the same as having a sync and async implementation in Polly v7.

I'm not sure what the best way to go about doing this natively for Polly v8 would be. Off the top of my head, it feels like we'd need a bridge interface that has sync and async methods so the strategy can just pick the right method and what happens under-the-hood is up to the implementation.

Doing the above means the policy can live in the core, but by default it wouldn't actually _do_ anything out of the box (which I think is also true of v7). We could then possibly have an additional assembly that will adapt from `IMemoryCache`/`IDistributedCache` to the policy cache interface. There'd possibly be some space for unintentional mistakes here though if someone setup a cache policy associated with `IDistributedCache` and then did a sync operation on it.

Using it via the extension would then be something like:

```csharp
// IMemoryCache
builder.AddCaching(
    MemoryCache.Default,
    (context, state) => /* some object */,
    (cacheEntry) => cacheEntry.SlidingExpiration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3));

// IDistributedCache
IDistributedCache distributedCache = ...;
builder.AddCaching(
    distributedCache,
    (context, state) => "my-cache-key",
    async (value) => await serializeToByteArray(value));
```

The other bit I wasn't 100% sure on was on exactly how to get the callbacks for generating the cache key and value to preserve `TResult` and `TState`.

Hey @martincostello, nice job :) just a couple of thoughts about the caching:

>Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Abstractions provides the sync IMemoryCache and the async IDistributedCache - this is effectively the same as having a sync and async implementation in Polly v7.

I believe the semantics are that `IDistributedCache` does not hold the cached locally while `IMemoryCache` does. The `IDistributedCache` is inherently slower and better scalable. When accessing/updating the `IMemoryCache` you don't need any async methods because all work is local. For `IDistributedCache` we have async overloads because it can indeed block the calling thread when making a request. However, `IDistributedCache` also exposes sync methods so we can use those when `ResilienceContext` is in synchronous execution. 

> I'm not sure what the best way to go about doing this natively for Polly v8 would be. Off the top of my head, it feels like we'd need a bridge interface that has sync and async methods so the strategy can just pick the right method and what happens under-the-hood is up to the implementation.

My naive thinking is that we expose two strategies `Distributed Caching Strategy` and `Memory Caching Strategy` each with their respective options. That way, the customer can compose these strategies and create 2-layerer caching strategies (memory first, followed by distributed caching). 

> Doing the above means the policy can live in the core, but by default it wouldn't actually do anything out of the box (which I think is also true of v7)

I think the main concern is imposing the `Microsft.Extensions.Caching.Abstractions` dependency on everyone if this was directly in the `Polly.Core`. My vote would be to have these strategies in `Polly.Caching` package (similar thing that we did with `Polly.RateLimiting`). That way the `Polly.Core` can stay slim.

> The other bit I wasn't 100% sure on was on exactly how to get the callbacks for generating the cache key and value to preserve TResult and TState.

I think we don't really need to propagate `TState`, it is reserved for advanced scenarios to reduce lambda allocations and I cannot image having anything caching-related in it. 

Regarding the API surface do you think we need these events?

``` csharp
    public Func<OnCacheHitArguments, ValueTask>? OnCacheHit { get; }

    public Func<OnCacheMissedArguments, ValueTask>? OnCacheMissed { get; }

    public Func<OnCachePutArguments, ValueTask>? OnCachePut { get; }
```

I think `OnCachePut` is nice to have so the caller can override any caching per-item options but the others might be not necesssary. We can still generate the resilience events from these though.

Based on the recent sync, the caching strategy won't be a part of the initial V8 release. If they're is a demand from community we might induce it in a next minor release. 

The reason to not include: 

- There is not much data about usability of such strategy or whatever it really belongs in a core resilience package.
- There is a work pending on the next set of caching libraries and we do not want to duplicate the work  or be based on older abstractions.

cc @martincostello ,@joelhulen

Per our conversation on Thursday, I agree that we can exclude the Polly v7 caching policy from v8. If we find that excluding the caching policy impacts a lot of people (no data on whether this is the case), then we can either find a way to implement it or provide some alternatives like the upcoming set of caching libraries.

I was directed here by [Martin Tomka](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/author/martintomka/) after I commented on the blog post [Building resilient cloud services with .NET 8](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/building-resilient-cloud-services-with-dotnet-8/#comment-20134). 

I work on a large enterprise application that is currently ASP.NET using Framework 4.8, with an effort underway to migrate to .NET 8+. We’re using the `IHttpClientFactory` to maintain a registry of named http clients with Polly v7 policies defined. 

We use a Polly `AsyncCachePolicy` on 6 of the ~75 named http clients we have defined for connecting to external APIs. This policy is backed by an `IAsyncCacheProvider` which is wired to use a Singleton `MemoryCacheProvider` in our DI container. The cache policy will serialize an HttpResponseMessage and cache that serialized representation in memory per-server.  In the case of a cache hit, we deserialize back to an HttpResponseMessage and return that. 

We knew there were trade-offs in this approach such as having to still `ReadAsAsync<T>` on the resulting `HttpResponseMessage` to further deserialize it into a DTO, but we felt the convenience of being able to define a generic caching policy to apply to a named http client was worth it in these cases. (In other words, we were aware of the guidance “[Is caching at the `HttpResponseMessage` level the right fit?](https://github.com/App-vNext/Polly/wiki/Polly-and-HttpClientFactory#is-caching-at-the-httpresponsemessage-level-the-right-fit)” )

In addition, we do have a handful of areas in our application where we use Polly’s Policy<T>.Execute() syntax with a caching policy to cache a DTO at a higher level than the http pipeline. 

To further complicate things, on the clients where we’re using the `AsyncCachePolicy`, it’s part of a Policy Wrap with `Polly.Contrib.DuplicateRequestCollapser` in order to avoid cache repopulation storms. There is an [issue on that package](https://github.com/Polly-Contrib/Polly.Contrib.DuplicateRequestCollapser/issues/8) that is in the process of being resolved where it initially didn’t support Polly v8. It looks like support for v8 is being added, but not Polly.Core. 

To recap, if my team wants to migrate from v7 to Polly.Core, in addition to the standard stuff outlined in the migration guide we’ll need to account for:
* Polly.Core not currently supporting a Cache strategy
* Polly.Core not providing an equivalent of `Polly.Contrib.DuplicateRequestCollapser`

Thanks,
-Brett.

If you are interested I may implement a policy based on [FusionCache](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache), which in turn can be configured to seamlessly work with both in memory and distributed caches (it has full support for both sync/async programming model, without the usual sync-over-async trick which does have its issues).

Honestly it was on my todo list for some time (I mean adding FusionCache support to Polly), but first I was waiting for Polly V8 to be released and then I've been sidetracked with some other stuff recently.

Hi @martintmk , I totally agree, I was not suggesting to add a hard link to FusionCache, that would be crazy.

The idea iwould be to have a caching abstraction specific for Polly with the specific requirements needed for Polly itself, so that various impl (including but of course not limited to FusionCache) can be made.

If, btw, there's currently no time to create such abstraction now, another possibility would be to start without the abstraction and try to see if it would be possible to get the caching feature as an external third party package, in this case tightly coupled with FusionCache, to get the feature out. Then, if and when the common abstraction will arrive, the package would be updated to work with the common abstraction. Just an idea.

Of course I would prefer the first approach, if possible.

ps: I'll look at your sample code asap, will let you know.

> Would your proposed approaches be something that would eventually make their way into the Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience package so they could be added to an HTTP Client definition? Or is the intent only to allow a cache strategy to be defined and incorporated into a standalone resilience pipeline that would be defined outside of the HTTP Client factory?

Any new API added to Polly is automatically available in `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`. This applies for caching too. When using `AddResilienceHandler` extension, the `AddCache` extension would be visible for `ResiliencePipelineBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>`.

One gotcha is that we can't serve the same instance of  `HttpResponseMessage` so some cloning/custom handling would possibly be required.

> One gotcha is that we can't serve the same instance of `HttpResponseMessage` so some cloning/custom handling would possibly be required.

Makes sense, and I think the approach would be similar to the one taken by OutputCache which basically does more or less the same thing (it caches http responses and serve a copy of them later).

Anyway if a discussion starts on the shape of the generic cache api for Polly, I'm available to discuss the details of it and provide a first implementation based on FusionCache as a third-party package.

Hey folks, just checking what's happening on the caching side. I must say that the `HybridCache` sounds pretty interesting. Do I understand that correctly that `FusionCache` can be implementation of `HybridCache`?

If that's true, what we could do (if `HybridCache` becomes popular), is to introduce `Polly.HybridCache` package with APIs tied to `HybridCache` abstractions.

One downside I see is that `HybridCache` does not expose synchronous APIs but we could bridge that by blocking.

@martintmk  The other thing hybrid cache does not allow is caches to introduce there own features. Therefore I think having a resilience strategy for caching would be a good thing in Polly.Core, even if it is no-op. I'm sure you came up with a prototype a while ago but can't find it.

Then Polly could provide a Polly.HybridCache package allowing @jodydonetti to provide a package specifically dedicated to Fusion Cache.

> Hey folks, just checking what's happening on the caching side. I must say that the `HybridCache` sounds pretty interesting. Do I understand that correctly that `FusionCache` can be implementation of `HybridCache`?

Hi @martintmk , basically yes but to be more precise: FusionCache will remain independent, it will not be reimplemented on top of HybridCache or depend on it, but it will **also** be available as an implementation of HybridCache (via an adapter class).
If interested, you can read about my thoughts about all of this [here](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/discussions/266#discussioncomment-9915972).

The upcoming [v2](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/milestone/15) will contain this and way more, and I recently released [preview-3](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/releases/tag/v2.0.0-preview-3) which contains the adapter class.
Nitpicking corner: currently in preview-3 there is a separate package, but I'll probably end up including the adapter in the main FusionCache package, but this is just a detail.

If you happen to play with it, please let me know!

> If that's true, what we could do (if `HybridCache` becomes popular), is to introduce `Polly.HybridCache` package with APIs tied to `HybridCache` abstractions.

That is one of the potential outcome, yes: as stated in my tought, if `HybridCache` becomes a shared abstraction for hybrid caches in .NET, packages may depend on it and then pick either the default Microsoft implementation **or** one of the available 3rd party ones, like FusionCache.

> One downside I see is that `HybridCache` does not expose synchronous APIs but we could bridge that by blocking.

Yup, that is one limitation.

Another one is that, even when using the FusionCache-based implementation through the HybridCache adapter, on one hand most FusionCache features will be available (like [fail-safe](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/FailSafe.md), [soft timeouts](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/Timeouts.md), etc), **but** on the other hand they will not be granularly controllable on a call-by-call basis since I'm limited by the `HybridCacheEntryOptions` class and what it offers (and that is why I'm planning a specific Polly implementation tied specifically for FusionCache, when you need more granular control).

Long answer, I know, but I wanted to give a clear enough overview in one place.

Hope this helps.

> @martintmk The other thing hybrid cache does not allow is caches to introduce there own features.

Kinda: as stated above new features may be introduced, but they'll be configurable only globally (eg: at setup time) and not on a call-by-call basis because of the `HybridCacheEntryOptions` limitations.

> I created a caching strategy for Hybrid Cache as it looks like a path forward for caching. [Axion.Extensions.Polly.Caching.Hybrid](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Axion.Extensions.Polly.Caching.Hybrid)

Hi @maksionkin , now that FusionCache v2 [has been released](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/releases/tag/v2.0.0), and since is both fully [compatible](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache/blob/main/docs/MicrosoftHybridCache.md) with Microsoft HybridCache and the [very first](https://x.com/jodydonetti/status/1881135481645339003) implementation of it that is [production-ready](https://x.com/stebets/status/1881361994340839832), would you mind checking if everything looks good with your caching strategy?

It may become a really useful addition to the toolset of Polly v8 users.

Let me know if I can be of help, thanks!

Re-opening after question in #2626, but marking as `help wanted`.

One additional consideration here is that `HybridCache` is an abstract implementation so you would likely use something like `FusionCache` as the actual implementation, so far, so good.

`FusionCache` already has stampede protection, however this only works at the L1 layer, i.e. 10 calls to Polly will result in only one going through to the API, but this does not address when you have multiple nodes, since these aren't aware of each other.

To solve this, you need the concept of a distributed lock, an example is [DistributedLock](https://www.nuget.org/packages/DistributedLock/) , now you can wrap the call to HttpClient in one of these, but it might be better to allow this as part of the Polly caching concept, so that it is all together.
